comments.text:
What a difference 3 years makes. I'm looking at a 3060 12GB for some entry level AI learning since they're cheap now at around $200 in mid 2024. I also put together my first system in probably close to 20 years after using laptops and older used enterprise equipment for non-gaming use.  

I ended up buying one of those overpriced 3090 cards, finding a Microcenter refurb with an additional 10% off, getting me the card for about $650 with tax. Coming back into system building after being gone for so long I was shocked to see $2000+ cards out there and $800-$1000 seemed to be the entry level norm. WOW!

I look back at some of these "lockdown" period videos and I'm shocked to see people paid so much for these mediocre cards. It reminds me of the cars for $20k over sticker during the worst parts of the shortages. During that time I was perfectly happy to be playing on my XBOX that I got used from GameStop for $150 and driving my then 6 year old car.

comments.text:
They are absolutely not artificially enhancing the shortage. If anything I wouldn't be surprised if Nvidea is rushing through development to make an extremely stripped down 30xx card that they can make as fast as possible.

Prices going up as supply dwindles is just basic economics. Every product works like that and it's sometimes a bit annoying that so many expect PC parts to somehow be exempt from that. Companies sell products for as much as people are willing to pay. That's just how capitalism works.
If Nvidea brings out a 800 dollar card and AMD a 600 dollar one and both are the same power people will go for the 600 one. But if neither cards are in stock people will pay what they are willing to pay since there is nothing cheaper to buy instead.


If anything though I do think profits for Nvidea and AMD are down because of all this. After all the prices are so high because there are far less cards being sold. Also with chips being used in so many products they themselves have to pay a massive premium for those as well since of course they are low in the picking order next to government projects and other industries like cars. GPU's are even considered below other PC parts like RAM and CPU which is why their shortage hasn't been anywhere near as bad.

comments.text:
In a free market, there is no prioritisation of essential services unless the government steps in and forces the issue. Moreover, I've never seen bleeding edge CPUs so cheap and readily available so I'm disinclined to buy the silicon shortage - especially considering that silicon is mined in the least likely places in the world to impose lockdowns. This, also, casts some doubt on the crypto-mining story too. The wholesalers saw a captive market, thanks to CoVID, got greedy, cranked up the prices then, well, time will tell but my money's on them getting caught with stock they can't unload. comments.text:
​ @MrMarinus18  There is no silicon shortage. A shortage of seawater would be more likely. Silicon is reduced from silica melt using carbon. Silica is the most abundant material in the earth's crust and silica mines draw from the purest reserves of any primary industry. So much so that if you pull a 99.50% assay on a prospect, it's still not nearly enough to be competitive. If African production so much as twitched, you'd have mines popping up all over the world, almost overnight. 

The rest is outdated. Vendors routinely deal with unstable market demand via a backorder system (where orders are placed before stock is manufactured) or, further down the chain, a pre-order system (where orders are placed before stock is delivered). It's no big deal and it's quite uncomplicated.

It is a fact that the big supply chains, in IT, have engaged in practices with criminal ramifications (bait and switch, reselling returns, selling seconds as new, lying to consumers about their rights, etc.) - and still do to this day - which you will discover if you ever order a good sample of memory in the mail. The DAG used for mineing limits what cards can mine, the dag needs increaseingly large vram reqs. use to be able to mine with 1-2-4 gb cards, but not anymore on alot of miners. and as time goes on the DAG requirements will grow, makeing the vram requirements go up for the card being used to  mine to be able to mine at all. comments.text:
V-RAM isn't just used for the frame buffer, Jay.

V-RAM capacity is ACTUALLY important even on low end systems for game engines that have borderless maps or otherwise progressively load and unload assets as you roam around the game. You know, like almost every game does these days. It's only going to get worse with the next gen console architectures.

A perfect example is Cyberpunk 2077. The detail density in the city makes differences painfully clear. If you have more vram, it'll load better textures, more unique npcs, more detail, etc. etc. ... and if you only want more performance? Well, ever notice stutters while a game is pulling an asset in to vram? Yea, doesn't happen if it's already in vram.

So to say more vram is pure marketing (even just at the low end) is ignorant. Completely ignorant.

... It's also why nvidia is dumb as hell for releasing their cards with so little RAM on some models. Must be desperate to keep gaming separate from work cards by literally nerfing the gaming cards.

The shuffle system is fucking terrible. It's the laziest and cheapest way for NewEgg to seem like it's doing something to fight scalpers without actually doing anything. There are plenty of other measures they could take to combat scalpers that would actually be effective but they would cost NewEgg money to develop and implement. The shuffle system is essentially a four lines of code random number generator. The scalpers still have the edge by a mile. People, like a few replying here, fixate on the one in a million chance they got a card while overlooking the months they spent in the shuffle and the millions of other people that never got through the shuffle. It's the same phenomena that causes people to believe in all those charlatans pretending to be psychics. (To be clear ALL psychics are charlatans.) They focus on the one time the shit heel was right and forget the thousand times they were wrong. 

You are playing NewEgg and the scalpers game. So the scalpers have to enter the shuffle with all the other purchasers. So what? It doesn't mean the playing field has been leveled. If it had been leveled people would have stopped bitching about not being able to get a card months ago when NewEgg first started the shuffle nonsense. If I am a scalper all I do to beat the shuffle is have my bot create a few thousand - or more - fake accounts. When one or more of those accounts come up in the shuffle I buy all I'm allowed to buy on that account. It wouldn't even cost me time because I could just set my computer to do the work while I sleep. In the end I still get all the cards I want and you will pay me for them on Amazon or sleazebay because that's the only way you're getting one until about late 2022 and it's not inconceivable that the shortage could even stretch into 2023 before availability gets back to pre-pandemic levels.

@JackoBanon1  why do people keep saying this? Why are crypto currency’s the future? 

Aside from it being a decentralized currency and a form of “electronic cash” if you will, it offers nothing more to consumers. 

I get that it’s “safer” than a centralized currency like the US dollar for example. But until they can figure out how to get transactions approved much much quicker, it will never be more that a backing for other currencies. Sure the transactions are more secure, but you’d be hard pressed to pass on the burden to consumers. 

I can swipe my visa, get approved, and be on my way in under 60 seconds. Can’t do that with crypto. And I think people are going to have an extremely tough time making crypto a mainstream currency, simply because SOMEONE will need to take a risk to get these transactions approved as quickly as credit cards. As of now in my opinion crypto is nothing more than an idea. An amazing idea for sure, but I’m still curious as to why everyone thinks this is “the future”

comments.text:
VRAM matters on low end if you are developing on a game engine. 

Try building production quality lighting in UE4 with 6GB VRAM... Well good luck! 

Low end GPUs with high VRAM are really nice to have for budget game developers.

For those who are wondering, yeah a crappy card can still be used in developing a game. Game engines generally crash during builds if you don't have enough RAM or VRAM, but your processing power only affects the time each build will take. Which is workable, as long as it doesn't crash at the end of a 3 hour lighting build because of memory overflow for example...

Drivers is software and the amount of times in January/February having to keep upgrading drivers to run a game was getting stupid. One week I had the latest drivers installed, the next another one comes out in Windows. 

Linux drivers for gaming has come an awful long way, but you still have to fiddle around to get rid of screen tearing, switching off  Sync To V Blank and Allow Flipping. Then going into the Advanced part and switching on, by ticking a box the Force Full Composition Pipeline, which basically switches off screen tearing when gaming, so no need for V-Sync to be switched on any more. Then you have to sort out DPI (Dots Per Inch) by adding a line to your xorg.conf file after saving your NVIDIA settings. Option         "DPI" "96 x 96" otherwise after rebooting with Force Full Composition on, you'll end up with a blank screen, won't be able to login. If you restart after saving your settings without Force Full Composition on, your fonts are really small, hence why we need to do the above with Force Full Composition and the Dots Per Inch settings. Now you would think that after all this time, especially now as Linux is only a few numbers away with NVIDIA Drivers from Windows, that NVIDIA would include the Dots Per Inch in the Drivers? comments.text:
One minor note about the 12GB VRAM; it's very niche, but livestreamers can put it to use. Running a rendering delay (to sync up input sources) GOBBLES VRAM, as the sources are stored uncompressed and full-frame pre-compositing in video memory (in OBS). The more VRAM you have, the longer delay you can use. Not much of a problem on a well-optimized system, but if you're using an old USB 2.0 video capture device with around 2 seconds of capture and transport latency in a real-time gameplay livestream setting, it would be invaluable. No more reacting 'ahead' of in-game events.
Of course the proper fix is to get a modern capture card (PCIe or USB 3.0) and not deal with a ridiculous delay in the first place, but if you're grabbing a 3060 you might not have that in the budget.
But! That VRAM can also be used for real-time compositing effects, looping delays, pixel shader buffer bashing, and other creative mutilations in a similar vein that love to just chew through a big stack of memory.

comments.text:
"12GB is a marketing gimmick"

Yes and no. The issue is that they had a choice between 6GB and 12GB, and the card likely benefits from having more than 6GB. The GPUs themselves are designed to address a certain number of VRAM channels, and they need 32 bit of bus per channel. 192 / 32 = 6. With 1GB per channel (like on the 3060Ti, 3070, & 3080) that comes to 6GB. With 2GB per channel (like on the 3090) that comes to 12GB. Those are their only options given the silicon that they have.

comments.text:
I think the "marketing circlejerk" thing may be wrong from what I've heard. 192-bit being the same as 3x 64-bit (where you can have 64-bit addressing to non-ECC memory ranks) would mean you could have: 512MBx3 = 1.5GB / 1GBx3 = 3GB / 2GBx3 = 6GB / 4GBx3 = 12GB -- but not 8GB or 16GB. It's the balance point, where 6GB wouldn't be enough, but 12GB would be a little overkill. Not being able to have access to 256-bit memory bandwidth (due to having to bin GPUs, some of which may not be usable with a 256-bit bus) would mean they would have to make this compromise.

EDIT: You do make a good point about the inability to use the extra memory due to people running it at a lower resolution with some of the newest games. Since people aren't making use of the extra memory size (smaller texture size), then it may not be worth them having more than 6GB VRAM on the cards. Then again, on some older games there is the possibility to use much more than 6GB VRAM and benefit from it while running 3840x2160. It's capable of running games at that resolution, and people are going to use that resolution. The 3060 would work well under those circumstances where people are running "4K", albeit with other graphics settings at a lower setting for the higher fps.

With only 8GB the Card would be severly bandwith starved, only having a 128bit bus, which is not enough for the 28SMs / 3584 shaders.  
6GB on the other hand fits well with a 192bit bus, but is the same as the  6 year old 1060 6G and the 2060 6G, which are  limiting already todays games at 1080p. So clearly 6Gb isn't enough in 2021. Nvidia could have pulled a GTX970 again with 8Gb total and only 6gb being fast and the other 2GB very slow, but remember the last time this ended up with them getting sued.

The card not being able to utilize its 12GB at all is clearly wrong.  there are scaling Tests which puts the 3060 ahead in several games vs the 3060ti  already at 1080p.  Especially when raytracing is enabled, the 8gb on the Ti und 3070 are limiting performance in watchdogs legion and minecraft RTX so much that the vanilla 3060 is up to 50% faster. https://www.pcgameshardware.de/Geforce-RTX-3060-Grafikkarte-277122/Specials/RTX-3060-Was-bringen-12-GByte-1367634/

This is the Card with RTX for the masses, the one many will be using for the next 5 or 6 years like the 1060 now. This will not be upgraded as frequently as a highend card like the 3080.  I think in this case 12gb make a lot of sense.

comments.text:
Yes, it sucks that we are not able to buy these new parts, and that it's being handled so poorly is also annoying, but what I'm also a little tired of is effectively blaming Nvidia and the IBPs and what not for the frankly unprecedented state of our society world wide, and in the same breath also blaming them for our clearly broken and deeply flawed global economy. 
Could they have handled the pricing better? Yes, obviously. Could they have built a product which makes more sense? It would seem that way. The amount of memory is a hella weird choice for damn sure.
But perhaps there was a missed opportunity here for a fresh take on, and bear with me and take a deep breath before I say: talk about how getting upset and cranky and frustrated at a time like this does nobody any good? and it might perhaps be more constructive to try and learn to accept the situation and remember that this too will pass. As is, this video comes off a little too much like a self-entitlement support group talk than a professional review of a product.
It's pointless to blame Nvidia or board partners for being a company with a goal to generate revenue and profit. Is it annoying? Fuck yes, but no matter the tantrums you pull, you won't change a damn thing about it. It is equally pointless to out our frustrations about the state of our collective existence on these companies, or on anyone else for that matter. It is not their fault.
Yes times are hard, and patience is at a premium, but perhaps we should realise that we too are making decisions under unprecedented circumstances, within most if not all of our lifetimes at least, and that perhaps we too are not making the smartest choices in how we are reacting to this situation, and maybe that is an opportunity for some self reflection we might benefit from.
Thank you for the video, and Im glad you're on the mend Jay. Take care and look forward to what you'll work on next!

The thing that confuses me is why so many seem to have the idea that PC parts should for some reason be exempt from how the economy works. I mean what good is "it should cost this" if nowhere is the price anything like that? PC parts are just like any other product; it's worth what the consumer thinks it's worth and that is by supply and demand. If they can get a cheaper one that works just as well then they won't buy it. However that's not the case. Rather the 2060 is older or not is totally irrelevant, it's not cheaper and that's all that matters.
Once AMD and Nividia get their stocks back up prices will drop. Again that's just how economy works.

Also the the whole 12GB being a marketing gimmick. I'm not so sure cause it's either 6GB or 12GB cause of the way it's designed.
Having a faster card with less RAM for gamers and a slower card with more RAM for content creators makes sense. That way they are not competing with themselves.

If you don't want to buy inflated prices, don't buy products when they are scarce.

comments.text:
@NebulonRanger  Wait until you're 60 or older. When your system is overwhelmed by medical tourism, your hospitals/staff aren't funded properly and there's just too many patients for not enough doctors, the doctors have to prioritize and the old are literally left to die. Also if treatment is too expensive (like aids), they won't allow you to pay more, even if you want to, and will, de facto, have to die.
The US might not be the best system in the world, but honestly, WITHOUT INSURANCE (in all caps because insurance causes the exact same issues: you lose your right to chose your treatment), USA is hands down the best system I've seen.
First because you can actually get the treatment that's super expensive and survive, versus not having the treatment. I'd rather be poor than dead. Second because of the high cost, it prevents abuse of the health system (people going to the hospital for a mild cold and clogging up the hospital).

I've worked a lot in many hospitals in the US and have seen with medicare/medicaid/insurance and without. I've seen France too where insurance through the state is mandatory (much like Canada).

Now from what I've seen in Canada (I help americans and french canadians communicate), the system is not overwhelmed YET. But with your policies on immigration, and low skills workers coming with low salaries (when they have a salary at all), it's just a matter of time before you become just like France and have to wait 8 hours before seing a doctor in the hospital because the whole world decided to get treated for free at your hospital.

There are many many things that should be said, like the myth that insurance and government intervention lowers medical costs when it's the exact opposite. With insurance, I would pay $800 for a trip at the ER (mandatory exams + copay of $250).

Without insurance, the same trup costs me $125 (the doctor can skip exams that are unecessary, and since the insurance doesn't fix the prices, the hospital is willing to lower the princes, it's called a sliding scale. So in the end insurance drives prices up, not down. Insurances, just like casinos, never lose money. You, the client, will always be the loser, no matter what lies they feed you. I paid more than $100 over MSRP for the 'Sapphire RX580 Nitro+ SE' I bought during the height of the bitcoin mining boom a few years back. (how many names can you give a single video card?). No way in hell am I shelling out anything for a card in the current market. Some of these GPUs cost more than the 19 year old near perfect condition four wheel drive truck I bought for my wife last year, and the truck will be useful for much longer than the GPU. 

Forget that the cards were overpriced to begin with. There's no excuse for the cards' MSRP to be as high as they are in the first place. No. Don't give me that shit about how it's a supercomputer that has more power than the CPU of the machine you're installing it in. 

Yeah, I know it's true, but show me how to leverage that for myself if I'm not rendering video (almost exclusively only available to NVIDIA cards) or mining some dodgy digital currency. 

You can't because it doesn't exist. Windows, Mac, Linux, none of them offload any CPU computing loads to the GPU under normal operations. Unused video RAM isn't made available for holding a bigger spreadsheet or holding more browser tabs. 

If you can't load an operating system on it, it's not a 'supercomputer', it's a fucking peripheral. And there's no valid reason it should cost as much or more than the entire rest of the computer.

JAY the dies are completely different, all 102 dies are the same within an architecture, same with 104 or 106 & onward each code is a different die. You cant just cut a 102 die in half and get say 2 106 dies. There are memory controllers, pcie and display out along the edges and the cores in the middle.
Although you can have a 104 die "limited/cut down" to 106 specs into a 106 card but the die would be 104 sized and should carry the "XX104" prefix. 
example - EVGA 2060 KO TU104-150 when 2060 was TU106-200

comments.text:
The reason it has 12Gb VRAM is because the 192bit bus can't address 8Gb at full speed. Nvidia had a choice between 6Gb and 12Gb VRAM. 6Gb isn't enough. That's fact.

8Gb VRAM would have been more expensive because it would require a larger 256bit bus. That means a larger die, lower yields, more traces on the PCB, more transistors. It would push the price up to the 3060Ti

The 3060 could have had 8Gb with a 192bit bus but the last 2Gb would have had to share it's bus with another module which would have reduced the bandwidth of anything over 6Gb by 50%. Just like they did with the gtx 970 where the last 0.5Gb had shared bandwidth.

So 12Gb VRAM is the best solution and not just a marketing circle jerk.

Why don't any of the tech channels understand bus speed addressing?

comments.text: jay just a heads up, more v-ram is really handy for being able to add more textures at higher resolutions to a game, these textures also include multiple version's of the same texture that are color coded differently to create the bump maps, normal maps, specular maps etc... each one of these "maps" is a separate texture that is loaded to the gpu's vram so the game engine has the information needed so it knows how to render each texture correctly when they interact with dynamic lights, in the games environment. the problem is with not having enough vram is you are now limited to the amount of textures you can have in the area or field of view and also the resolution of those textures. more v-ram is better with out a doubt and its the only way you going to get next gen visuals without a big performance hit to fps compared to rtx or a game that uses heavy workloads of shaders in the game. hd textures are the cheapest way to decorate a game's environment and make it look good and look next gen. think of a games environment as a 3d photo if you had the ability to 3d scan a small city block and you had the v-ram capability of holding terabytes of storage. you could use a 1 single mega texture to cover the whole area and have the visuals of 16k resolution, things will start to look very realistic very quick and the performance hit will not really be noticeable as once the texture is loaded the game only has to display the image as its just a picture applied to a 3d object.

I actually like the Newegg shuffle.. because it's the ONLY chance I even have to get one of the new products.   After having alerts running for over a month before giving up, I wish more e-tailers followed suite.

And I also disagree with all the reviewers discrediting the 12GB VRAM on the cards.  Sure, the card isn't meant for 4k, but it's not like it can't do it (especially with DLSS).  And regardless, having the VRAM buffer lets you use high quality settings in games (notably 4K texture packs which chew through VRAM), where your resolution *does not matter*.  It also provides benefits outside of gaming as well.  Really, no card should be coming out with less than 10GB VRAM at this point in time; it significantly lowers its value and future proofing capability.  AMD is doing it right, and forcing NVIDIA to try to match them; and the 3060 vs the 3060 Ti shows this in spades.  Makes NV look like the doofus instead for once.

comments.text:
Sorry, but as happens sometimes, Jay is just wrong. 12GB might not be "necessary", but it is far from "nothing but a PR move". 

The fact is, no matter how slow the bus, it's still far faster than fetching stuff you've had to store in system RAM because you ran out of VRAM. The usefulness will certainly vary, and you can argue you could just lower textures etc. But straight up running out of VRAM is far more detrimental than just losing FPS on account of not keeping up with processing. 

12GB on this card makes it last longer, end of story. You can keep dropping resolution or post processing effects etc to make up for the processing power. But if you ever simply don't have enough VRAM to play with anymore, there's nothing you can do.

If you buy a new card every year, very unlikely this will ever affect you. But if you hold on to cards for longer then this gives it a longer life, so long as you can deal with less and less frames/less and less fanciness. 

Lastly, as far as I can tell, GDDR6 is fabbed on 10nm, so doesn't affect the 7/8nm nodes that nVidia and AMD fabricate their stuff on. Intel does fab on 10nm, but at least for now they have their own fabs, so this isn't the same pool of silicon.

EDIT: I'd just like to add that I do think AMDs 16GB of VRAM is a much better target for "purely PR". That amount of needed VRAM is so far off in the future that it is unnecessary. I think they would have been much better off with 12GB also. That said, GDDR6 is so cheap, I don't really mind. But they are a much better target than this 12GB for playing PR games.

3060 is a waste of money, a mockery by Nvidia

The MSRP for the 2060 at launch was set to 349 bucks, but after the release of Super variants, the MSRP was decreased to 299$.
So +10% of price, for around 20% better performance with this 3060.
Same tier performance of 2060 Super, same tier of price.
But, in the real world with scalped price, the cost will be higher even in comparison with 2070 Super, that is defenetely faster.
Further, while 3060 Ti have slightly better performance than 2080 Super (399 vs 699 MSRP), 3060 have slighlty better performance of the 2060 Super (329 vs 399), this after adopting new node and architecture.
Even the efficiency is nearly the same (170 vs 175 Watt of TDP).
Other datas: 3060 Ti, with 25% lower price than the 3070, have only 10% less the performance. 
3060 with 21% lower price than 3060 Ti, have 25% to 30% less the performance, so the performance/cost ratio is worse. If we consider that GA106 is way smaller than GA104, and that GA106-300 used for 3060 is a cut-down of the full chip (32 vs 28 SMs), they charging premium price on a lower-end product, that is simply ridicolous, a really shame.

comments.text: The only options available to a 192-bit design are 6GB VRAM or 12GB VRAM. For $329, in 2021, consumers would simply see a 6GB card as insulting. The 1060 released 4.5 years ago for $249 with 6GB. The RTX 2060 released 2 years ago for $299 with 6GB. And the 2060 Super, which this should really be replacing, has 8GB, and much more memory bandwidth. It's true that 8GB is enough for the vast majority of gaming workloads, and 6GB isn't too bad. But AMD didn't go with 16GB VRAM just for marketing purposes. It's partially just a forward thinking move (finewine), and partially because they knew they couldn't put 6GB on their down market cards. But another chunk of the equation is that they're hoping to gain mindshare and marketshare in GPU-compute. They don't segment or lock down their gaming vs. workstation cards nearly as much as NVidia does. The only way people with certain workloads (3D modeling, 4K/8K encoding, deep learning) can get a card that might meet their needs without spending ~$2k+ on a 3090 or Quadro is to go AMD. Or at least that was the plan before the crypto necromancers got busy again.

Second, it doesn't require you to slam a web site at some arbitrary instant -- with 100000 others -- to try to have a chance.  Like trying to get a good position on a Southwest Airlines flight.  It really is one of the better ideas.  But I hate that it is so opaque.  We don't know how many units are available, how many people we are up against (generally, what our chances are), and they do not ever announce it in advance, despite that it would be easy to do so. At this point, I feel like the only way to get a new card is to suck it up and stand in line :/ 
Best buy literally wouldn't even update for me until 18min AFTER and that's when I found them to be out of stock. Ridiculous!

I'm coming from a 765 GTX M so ANYTHING would have been better and yes I did react out of desperation but before my standing in line experience at MicroCentre, I didn't know if I was going to be able to get a card at all.

I went to MicroCentre around 1830 and a line started around 2300. Around 0700, I guess the stockers showed up and informed us there were cards instock (150 of them!) and since I was 7th in line, I knew I would get one AND have a choice of which SKU. I shamelessly chose the Gaming X at 512usd.
My point is that, if you REALLY want a card, going to a store might be the only way to secure one. Also, super important above all, make sure you're no more than 20th in line. Any position after 20 in line and you risk not getting anything on launch day if they don't have many cards; just my 2cents.

I understand not everyone has the luxury of doing the 1.5 day line wait but if you have someone willing to do so or if you know a line waiting service (don't know what they're officially called, I know there are services where you can pay someone to do the line wait for you) I'd say those would be your best options.

As for the Ti versions of the '70 and '80, you bet your ass I'll make it priority to be first in line on those release days because lay Jay explained, I can imagine that those models would be in very short supply on launch day (just my hypothesis).

comments.text:
The fact that product reviewers like JTC, LTT, GN and Hardware Unavailable are now barely receiving the products to review pretty much illustrates the problem. They've all received the same base model, bottom of the stack, EVGA 3060 XC Black, the cheapest card available, from Nvidia directly, not the AIBs, because the AIBs know that right now they don't need any help to sell the products. Anything available will sell instantly, regardless of where it lies in the product stack and how it compares to its peers and at a massively inflated price to boot.

I suspect the only reason Nvidia has sent these bottom rung cards out to reviewers is to essentially keep the channel open, as it were. They're at least considering the future somewhat, and want to maintain the minimum level of back-and-forth between themselves and the PC Enthusiast community.

Obviously recovering from Covid-19 takes priority, but if you're feeling run-down over the whole GPU situation, what about changing your focus towards products that are available? I particularly enjoyed your review of the Azza Overdrive, your case reviews are much easier to 'digest' than GN for example. You mentioned the possibility of doing a build in that in the video. The XOC videos with the Kingpin 3090s are also entertaining.

Maybe do a video about Power Supplies? It's something that's often overlooked and not properly understood by a lot of people. Break down features like undervolt protection and how that can affect your system if you don't have it. I know they're pretty obvious but there's the pros and cons of modular and non-modular, how modular is typically a little more expensive but neater and allows for things like cable-mod cables, non-modular can be easier for the inexperienced but might not have all the PCI-E power cables you need if you've got, say, a triple 8 pin GPU. The difference between ATX, SFX and SFX-L. The length can be a factor in some cases, like my MSI Gungnir 100; if the PSU is longer than 180mm you're going to have to remove the 3.5" drive bay, thereby limiting your storage options.

comments.text:
Oh it gets worse. Cars weren't selling last year so the manufacturers prioritized electronics, including consumer electronics believe it or not.

But when the component orders have to be placed ahead of time, often in weeks. Then shipped over on a massive diesel cargo ship. The problem cascades into months.

It doesn't help that Toyota popularized JIT (just in time) manufacturing techniques a while back. Everyone stopped maintaining inventory in favor of cost and "efficiency". Everything computerized... orders placed sometimes months ago timed to arrive in a holding area just before use.

A pandemic hit, and nobody was left holding enough inventory to push through even PART of it.

JIT manufacturing was great for profit margins. It was nice for companies that didn't want to be left holding large, unsold inventories, but as we can all clearly see, it isn't resilient to even moderate supply chain disruption.

comments.text:
Actually I believe 3060 chip (GA106) is not a cut down/lower bin chip from anything that Nvidia have released so far. 3090 and 3080 share the same chip (GA102), 3070 and 3060 ti share the same chip (GA104). So they produced this chip specifically to target the mid low to low end market (although even at MSRP, $330 is hardly a mid low pricing for most people). 3050 probably will use this same chip, but right now, only 3060 is using GA106. So saying that Nvidia making this because of left over or something is probably not correct. For people wondering why they have these different chips instead of using 1 chip and bin it aggressively, the problem is that the supply is going to be too unreliable. If 30% good enough for 3090, 50% good enough for 3080, then what? you're left with 20% to make 3070, 3060 ti and 3060. That is simply not enough. You can balance it by potentially selling chip that perform better to be use on the lower tier product, but that is basically throwing away money (it has been done before tho, but normally they want to avoid this). Also by using 1 chip (so basically using the biggest chip) then it will be harder to make it cheap, also will be harder to produce it in quantity. The chip size (die size) for GA102 is 628 mm², GA104 392 mm², GA106 276 mm². By producing several chips tailored to different tier they can make more GPUs and price it accordingly.
As for shuffle, depending on how it's done, it is actually a good thing. It is actually a lot more fair using the shuffle vs first come first serve. First come first serve is not something you want to do for items that is going to be limited in quantity. As long as the store can make sure that there is not going to be a duplicate buyer (in Japan, they do this by using your ID), then everyone can take their time to apply for the product and wait for the result. This way they can avoid large scale scalpers and stop people from being glued to the store/keep pressing F5. Yes, it is definitely a hassle, especially for people that actually need a new GPU right now, but unless you have some unicorn system that can tell this person deserve more than the other person, having a shuffle/lottery is not something you should dismiss unless you actually have a better solution that can be more fair to everyone.

comments.text: Just want to point out, these cards are not low performing versions of previous dies, just cut down because they did not make the cut for the higher tier.  The 3060 is the only GA106 based card nvidia is making currently, the 3060ti actually is a cut down GA104, and 3080 is a cut down GA102.  Nvidia benefits because the smaller dies generally have a significantly better yield so they could theoretically make a lot more cards with the same amount of silicon, though we probably will see some 3050ti or something like that as a cut down GA106 to make money on the few chips that have some issues.  (This is also likely true for AMD, the upcoming whatever will be based on the Navi 22 die, not the much larger Navi 21 that the 6800, 6800XT, and 6900XT are all on)  Overall agree with the main thrust of the video though.  The computer market is completely borked right now to the point that I postponed refreshing my desktop because of parts availability and cost.

comments.text: Correct me if I am wrong, but from my understanding, the 3060 has 12GB of VRAM because of it's 192 bit memory bus, unlike it's Ti counterpart with has the 256 bit memory bus. I once read a few years ago that each 32 bits of memory bus connects to one package of GDDR, which is manufactured in amounts of power at either 1GB or 2GB. Although you could technically use 8 GB VRAM with the 3060, it would lead to non-uniform performance. With a 192 bit bus, the ideal configurations are either 6GB or 12GB of VRAM. If you divide 192 by 32, you get 6. If you multiply 6 by the GDDR packages of 1GB or 2GB, you get 6GB or 12GB of VRAM. So I guess where I am going with this is, is it purely a marketing strategy, or was it partly due the GA106 not likely being able to take advantage of the 256bit bus?

comments.text:
It isn't "capitalism" when it isn't a free market, and atm we do not by any means whatsoever have a free market, re the vast plethora of govt restrictions in the supply chain, delays to shipment procedures, border control policies, staggering levels of govt printed/borrowed money which is inflating the market, etc. So place the blame where it truly lies: pandemics do not cause shortages, govt responses to them do.

As for "scalpers", again that's just an excuse to dodge where the core responsibility lies in the demand cycle, namely, with the buyer. Market situations such as this are demand-driven; it's not scalping to raise prices to control demand. If you stop retailers from raising prices as they should be able to (free market) then by definition that facilities a margin gap which will be exploited, and you don't get to decide what someone does with a product they buy. Price fixing creates black markets and price distortion, it always has, whether it's done via govt edict or consumer/media pressure. In a demand-dominated market, you have to choose between higher standard pricing or black markets, so stop complaining about govt policies and consumer behaviour which block the former and encourage the latter at the same time.

https://libertarianinstitute.org/articles/why-price-gouging-actually-helps-during-a-crisis/

This stuff is 101, Jayz. Atm the only channel which explains it properly is Bryan of Tech Yes City. Paul of NAAF touches on it too sometimes, but not so deeply as Bryan, though Tom of MLID has explained many times how all the companies are exploiting what's going on for their own gain. As long as consumers are willing to pay the prices though, and as long as they have spare cash to burn for all sorts of reasons (I recall people referring to stimulus cheques as, "2080 Ti tickets"), then this cycle will not end. Those who complain about price increases but at the same time accept govt handouts which they spend on non-essential tech products are being very hypocritical, their actions are adding to the inflationary pressures. I've seen many PC parts prices in the last 3 months increase by the equivalent of as much as 500% p/a.

Don't even get me started on crypo... :\

https://static.coindesk.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Bitriver-farm-710x458.jpg

https://www.calcalistech.com/ctech/articles/0,7340,L-3733744,00.html

One cannot artificially cap demand; criticising AIBs and retailers responding to all these pressures is just dumb (you are aware that these companies have all sorts of increased costs, yes? They have to pay more for the restricted supply options, and these custom web site changes don't appear out of thin air). Atm the only things that can really help are an end to the stupid  lockdowns & restrictions and the reopening of normal supply chains. Some believe that a crypto crash would be a solution, but that his its own serious consequences in other ways (because govts and conventional investors are now spending big on crypto aswell).

comments.text:
Jay has been putting out a lot of videos with false information lately.  Leaks have been verified many times over that the 6700xt will release with 12gb of vram, not 16.  Also, each die is made together (GA102, GA106, etc) and yields are only split between dies, so a bad binned GA102 will not be used as a GA106.  Nvidia may still use a bad binned GA102 for a GPU that would use a GA106 (the 2060ko was a TU104 die cut down to a 2060 core count, which is why it performed much better than other 2060 cards in blender)

I also find his view on Newegg shuffle to be a privileged view.  It's his opinion, so I don't argue with him stating it.  But it's a privilege to be able to be able to wait for a release the moment it happens, and the newegg shuffle helps to remove some of this privilege by expanding the window of opportunity to buy to a few hours instead of a few....seconds?

I do absolutely agree that the larger VRAM sizes are out there more as marketing, though certain workloads may need the VRAM more than the compute power and the 3060 is a great opportunity for those people.
